title.text: Blood alcohol thresholds and the law

why_how.text: The drinking driver is the number one cause of fatal traffic crashes, and on average someone is killed by a drunk driver every forty minutes.

It is against the law to drive under the influence of alcohol or other drugs, because drinking or drugged drivers lack good control of themselves and the vehicle and endanger their own lives and others.

Vermont law treats a driver with a blood alcohol concentration of point zero eight or above as under the influence or impaired, but a person is impaired below that level too, and even one drink impairs judgment.
Point zero eight is the blood alcohol level at which any driver is legally impaired, while point zero two is the level that already earns a driver under twenty-one a civil violation and suspension.

A driver under twenty-one with an alcohol concentration of point zero two or more can receive a civil traffic violation, has the license suspended and must complete an alcohol and driving education program at personal expense.

title.text: Implied consent, suspension and conviction consequences

why_how.text: A conviction for driving under the influence or after taking drugs brings license suspension, a large fine, lawyer fees, payment for an alcohol education class, possible jail and higher insurance.

Vermont's implied consent law means that by getting a license a person agrees to take a test for alcohol or drugs when a police officer who suspects impairment asks, and refusing the test costs the license for at least six months.
Refusing the implied consent test costs the license for at least six months on its own, separate from any penalty for a driving under the influence conviction.
Vermont has an administrative suspension process, so a license can be lost through a civil process before any criminal conviction for driving under the influence.
Administrative suspension is a civil loss of the license that can happen before a criminal conviction, whereas the conviction itself brings the fine, class, possible jail and insurance increase.

title.text: What alcohol does and how long

why_how.text: Alcohol is a drug and a depressant that affects the thought process and does not give a lift, and the decisions made after drinking may well be faulty.

Alcohol harms judgment so you no longer make good driving decisions or sense the risks you take, reduces overall vision, lets the mind wander so you cannot concentrate, and lowers comprehension so you may not realize what you are doing.

Alcohol suppresses the senses so you do not feel speed and may speed without knowing it, and it lengthens reaction time so moving the foot from gas to brake takes longer, which can be the difference between arriving safely or not at all.

Time is the only way to reduce the effects of alcohol, coffee, a cold shower or running around will not sober anyone up, and the body needs at least an hour per drink to process the alcohol, so several hours may pass before driving is safe.
Only time at a rate of at least an hour per drink reduces alcohol's effects, and coffee, cold showers and exercise change nothing but how awake you feel.
Coffee, a shower or exercise cannot lower blood alcohol concentration or its effects; only time does, at a minimum of an hour per drink.

why_how.text: The Vermont Emergency Nurses Association sponsors signs at the sites of alcohol related fatal crashes, and each sign marks a place where someone died because of a drunk driver.
A person worried about their drinking can contact the Vermont Helplink, a free and confidential alcohol and drug support and referral service run by the Department of Health.

Many crashes each year happen because a driver falls asleep at the wheel, often ending in a head on crash with another vehicle, a tree or a roadside object, and drowsy drivers can drive so poorly that they appear drunk.
Signs of drowsy driving are trouble focusing or keeping the eyes open, repeated yawning, not remembering the last few miles, drifting out of the lane and missing traffic signs.

People most at risk of drowsy driving are those who drive without enough sleep, often young people, shift workers, people working very long hours and people who may not know they have a sleep disorder, and a driver who believes they can stay awake may fall asleep and crash instead.

Avoid driving when drowsy, and if drowsiness strikes on the road find a safe place to pull over and stop, because opening the window or turning up the radio will not keep you awake and looking for ways to stay awake is itself the sign to stop and rest.
A drowsy driver can look like a drunk driver to others, but the remedy for drowsiness is to pull over and sleep, not to open a window or raise the radio.

title.text: Drugs and planning a safe ride

why_how.text: Impairment is not limited to alcohol: drugs, including prescription and over the counter medicines, can seriously affect driving, and drowsy driving is also dangerous.

Driving after taking other drugs or narcotics, even prescription or over the counter ones, can be as deadly as alcohol or deadlier for some people, since drugs can cause sleepiness and poor thinking, and time is again the only remedy.

If you plan to drink, plan first: use a designated driver who agrees not to drink or use drugs and takes responsibility for getting everyone home, or call a parent or other responsible person for a safe ride.

Other safe plans are to stay overnight where you are if it is safe, to take friends seriously when they warn you not to drive, and to hand your keys before drinking to a non drinking friend who will not let you drive.
